Introduction

The question of how the United States should address the estimated 11–12 million undocumented immigrants residing within its borders is one of the most consequential policy debates of our time. A nation that cannot control who enters and remains within its borders is not truly sovereign. The ability to determine membership in the national community is among the most fundamental attributes of statehood. By allowing millions of people to reside in the country outside the bounds of legal authorization, the United States effectively cedes a portion of that sovereign authority.

Advocates for the undocumented population frequently claim that these individuals contribute to the economy through labor and consumption. While there is some truth to this, the full fiscal picture is far less favorable than proponents suggest.

Numerous studies, including those by the National Academy of Sciences and the Center for Immigration Studies, have documented that low-skilled immigrants—documented and undocumented alike—consume more in government services (education, healthcare, emergency services, law enforcement, and public infrastructure) than they contribute in taxes. While the vast majority of undocumented immigrants are not security threats, the simple reality is that a system that cannot account for millions of people within its borders is a system with dangerous blind spots. If the government cannot credibly remove those with no legal right to remain, it effectively cedes a core sovereign function. Mass deportation, carried out lawfully, is not an act of hostility but an assertion that the American people, through law, determine who may enter and stay. It clarifies that immigration is a privilege conferred by a democratic process, not a fait accompli established by unlawful presence.

Security, broadly understood, also argues for decisive enforcement. The vast majority of migrants are not threats, but large-scale unlawful entry and visa overstay make it harder to verify identities, screen for risks, and dismantle smuggling networks. A system that cannot or will not remove those here illegally incentivizes the very black markets—fake documents, human trafficking, wage theft—that prey on migrants and erode public safety. Consistent removals, integrated with employer sanctions and robust identity verification, deny criminal enterprises the oxygen of impunity and help restore integrity to the immigration system.

Economically, mass deportation is often caricatured as self-defeating, yet the long-term benefits of restoring legality are substantial. An underground labor market depresses wages, especially for the least advantaged workers, and rewards businesses that cut corners at the expense of law-abiding competitors. Enforcing removals in tandem with mandatory E-Verify and serious penalties for illegal hiring levels the playing field. It reduces exploitation, encourages investment in training and technology, and aligns labor demand with lawful, regulated supply—whether via employment visas, seasonal worker programs, or domestic workforce development. Temporary dislocations are real, but they are the predictable result of ending a subsidy for illegality; transitional policies can mitigate them while preserving the principle that work in the United States must be authorized.

Public planning also benefits from clarity. Schools, hospitals, housing, and infrastructure depend on accurate population counts and legal status information for budgeting and eligibility. Persistently high levels of unlawful presence complicate these tasks and can strain services in ways that local governments cannot effectively manage. Ensuring that those who remain are lawfully present improves fiscal predictability and enables targeted assistance where it is both lawful and most needed.

  • Robust visa overstay tracking and timely removals.

Model Response:

The Case for Strict Enforcement: Why Mass Deportation of Undocumented Immigrants Is a Policy Imperative

Introduction

The question of how a nation addresses the presence of millions of individuals residing within its borders in violation of its laws is not merely an administrative matter—it is a defining test of national sovereignty, democratic governance, and the rule of law itself. The United States currently hosts an estimated 11 to 12 million undocumented immigrants, a population that has grown over decades as successive administrations have failed to meaningfully enforce existing immigration statutes. While the prospect of mass deportation is often dismissed as impractical or inhumane, a serious examination of the principles at stake reveals that comprehensive enforcement—including the removal of those who have entered or remained in the country illegally—is not only justified but necessary. The integrity of the legal system, the sovereignty of the nation, the fairness owed to legal immigrants, the economic well-being of American workers, and the security of the homeland all demand that the United States take decisive action to enforce its immigration laws without selective exception.

I. The Rule of Law as the Foundation of Democratic Society

The most fundamental argument in favor of mass deportation is the principle that laws must be enforced to retain their meaning. Immigration law in the United States is not ambiguous. Federal statutes establish clear procedures for legal entry, define the conditions under which foreign nationals may reside and work in the country, and prescribe consequences for violations. When millions of people live in open defiance of these statutes without consequence, the rule of law itself is undermined.

The rule of law is not an abstract philosophical concept—it is the operational foundation of a democratic republic. It requires that laws apply equally to all persons and that the government does not exercise arbitrary discretion in choosing which laws to enforce and which to ignore. When the executive branch effectively nullifies immigration law through non-enforcement, it usurps the legislative authority of Congress, which enacted those laws through the democratic process. Citizens who voted for representatives who passed immigration legislation are effectively disenfranchised when the executive branch refuses to carry out the law.

Critics often argue that enforcement discretion is a normal feature of governance, and that prosecutorial resources must be allocated strategically. This is true in the context of individual cases where discretion is exercised within a framework of general enforcement. But what has occurred in the United States is not discretionary prioritization—it is a de facto policy of mass non-enforcement that has rendered entire categories of law functionally void. When non-enforcement becomes the norm rather than the exception, it ceases to be discretion and becomes nullification.

Moreover, selective non-enforcement creates a corrosive precedent. If immigration law can be ignored with impunity, citizens may reasonably ask why other laws should command their respect. The social contract depends on mutual obligation: citizens obey laws they may personally disagree with because they trust that the legal framework applies equally and is enforced consistently. When the government signals that certain laws are merely aspirational—suggestions rather than mandates—it erodes the civic trust upon which self-governance depends.

Mass deportation, understood as the systematic enforcement of existing removal orders and immigration statutes, is simply the government fulfilling its most basic obligation: executing the law as written. To frame this as radical is to accept the extraordinary premise that the default condition of governance should be lawlessness.

II. National Sovereignty and Border Integrity

Sovereignty, in its most elemental form, is the right of a political community to determine who may enter its territory, reside within its borders, and participate in its civic life. This principle is universally recognized in international law. Every nation on earth maintains immigration laws, and every nation reserves the right to remove individuals who violate those laws. The United States is not exceptional in this regard, nor should it be expected to be.

The concept of national borders is not an arbitrary relic of a less enlightened era. Borders delineate the jurisdiction within which a self-governing people exercises democratic authority. The citizens of the United States, through their elected representatives, have established the terms under which foreign nationals may enter and remain. When those terms are violated on a mass scale and the government fails to respond, the practical meaning of sovereignty is diminished.

Open-borders advocates sometimes argue that national borders are morally illegitimate constraints on human freedom. But this position, if taken seriously, would dissolve the very concept of the nation-state and, with it, the framework of democratic self-governance. If the United States has no legitimate authority to control who resides within its borders, then it has no legitimate authority to levy taxes, enforce criminal law, or conduct any of the other functions that depend on territorial jurisdiction. Sovereignty is not divisible in this way: a nation either controls its borders or it does not fully govern itself.

Mass deportation is an assertion of this sovereign authority. It communicates to the world that the United States takes its own laws seriously, that its borders are meaningful, and that entry into the country is a privilege extended on terms established by the American people through democratic processes—not a right to be claimed unilaterally by anyone who manages to evade detection.

Furthermore, the failure to enforce immigration law creates perverse incentives that perpetuate illegal immigration. When potential migrants observe that millions of people have entered the United States illegally and remained without consequence—and in many cases have received public services, employment, and even legal protections—the rational calculation favors illegal entry over the often lengthy and burdensome legal immigration process. Comprehensive enforcement, including deportation, is necessary to break this cycle and restore the credibility of the immigration system.

III. Fairness to Legal Immigrants

One of the most overlooked dimensions of the immigration debate is the profound injustice that non-enforcement inflicts on those who have followed the law. Every year, millions of people around the world apply for legal admission to the United States. They fill out forms, pay fees, submit to background checks, wait in lines that can stretch for years or even decades, and comply with every requirement imposed upon them. Many are separated from family members for extended periods. Many are denied entry altogether.

When the government tacitly permits millions of people to bypass this process entirely, it sends an unmistakable message: the legal immigration system is for those who lack the initiative or willingness to break the law. The person who waits patiently for a visa is, in effect, punished for their compliance, while the person who crosses the border illegally or overstays a visa is rewarded with de facto residency.

This is not justice. It is a system that penalizes law-abiding behavior and incentivizes violation. Any policy that claims to value immigration must begin by honoring the sacrifices and patience of those who respected the process. Mass deportation of undocumented immigrants is not anti-immigrant—it is pro-legal-immigrant. It affirms that the legal pathway to residency and citizenship has value, and that those who followed it made the right choice.

Amnesty proposals, by contrast, compound the injustice. Granting legal status to those who entered illegally effectively retroactively validates the decision to break the law and penalizes those who chose to comply. If the United States has any obligation to fairness in its immigration system, that obligation runs first to those who respected its laws.

IV. Economic Considerations and the Protection of American Workers

The economic effects of illegal immigration are contested, but several points are difficult to dispute. The presence of a large undocumented labor force exerts significant downward pressure on wages in low-skill industries, including construction, agriculture, food processing, and service sectors. The workers most affected by this pressure are not affluent professionals but the most economically vulnerable Americans—those without college degrees, including disproportionate numbers of Black and Hispanic citizens.

The basic economics are straightforward: when the supply of labor increases in a given sector without a corresponding increase in demand, wages fall. Undocumented immigrants, because of their legal vulnerability, are often willing to accept wages and working conditions that would be unacceptable to legal workers. This does not reflect a moral failing on the part of undocumented workers, but it does create a structural dynamic that harms American workers and legal immigrants who compete in the same labor markets.

Proponents of illegal immigration often argue that undocumented workers do jobs that Americans are unwilling to do. This claim misunderstands labor economics. There are no jobs that Americans are categorically unwilling to perform—there are only wages that are insufficient to attract American workers. If the supply of undocumented labor were removed, employers in affected industries would be compelled to raise wages, improve working conditions, and invest in productivity-enhancing technology. This would benefit American workers and create a more honest and sustainable labor market.

Additionally, undocumented immigrants impose fiscal costs on state and local governments. While they contribute to the economy through consumption and, in some cases, tax payments, studies consistently show that the fiscal costs of public education, emergency healthcare, law enforcement, and other services consumed by undocumented populations exceed their tax contributions, particularly at the state and local level. These costs are borne by American taxpayers, including many who are themselves struggling economically.

Mass deportation would tighten labor markets in low-skill sectors, increase wages for the most vulnerable American workers, reduce fiscal burdens on state and local governments, and create conditions under which legal immigration could be calibrated to meet genuine economic needs.

V. National Security and Public Safety

The inability to account for millions of individuals residing in the country without documentation represents a significant national security vulnerability. This is not to suggest that undocumented immigrants are disproportionately likely to be criminals or terrorists—most are not. But a rational security policy cannot be indifferent to the presence of a large population that has not been vetted through any screening process.

Legal immigration involves background checks, security screenings, and identity verification. These procedures exist for a reason: to ensure that individuals admitted to the country do not pose a threat to public safety. When millions of people bypass these procedures, the government has no way of knowing who they are, where they come from, or whether they have criminal histories or affiliations with hostile organizations.

Moreover, the infrastructure of illegal immigration—smuggling networks, fraudulent document industries, and unsecured border corridors—is exploited by criminal organizations engaged in drug trafficking, human trafficking, and other serious crimes. The normalization of illegal border crossing creates an environment in which dangerous actors can operate alongside economic migrants, making it more difficult for law enforcement to identify and interdict genuine threats.

Comprehensive enforcement, including deportation, would reduce the size of the unvetted population, disrupt the criminal networks that facilitate illegal immigration, and allow law enforcement and intelligence agencies to focus their resources on genuine security threats rather than managing the consequences of mass non-enforcement.

VI. Addressing the Practicality Objection

The most common objection to mass deportation is that it is logistically impractical and prohibitively expensive. This objection deserves serious engagement, but it is ultimately unpersuasive.

First, the fact that enforcing a law is difficult does not relieve the government of the obligation to enforce it. Many areas of law enforcement are expensive and logistically challenging—combating organized crime, enforcing environmental regulations, prosecuting financial fraud—but no serious person argues that the difficulty of enforcement justifies abandoning the effort. The scale of the problem is a reflection of decades of neglect, not an argument for continued neglect.

Second, mass deportation need not involve dramatic military-style operations. A significant portion of the undocumented population could be induced to leave through consistent enforcement of existing laws. Mandatory E-Verify for all employers, combined with meaningful penalties for hiring undocumented workers, would eliminate the primary economic incentive for illegal residence. When employment opportunities dry up, many undocumented immigrants would choose to return to their home countries voluntarily—a process sometimes described as "self-deportation" or "attrition through enforcement." This approach, combined with the vigorous execution of existing removal orders and the deportation of those encountered through routine law enforcement, would substantially reduce the undocumented population over time without requiring a single massive operation.

Third, the cost of deportation must be weighed against the ongoing costs of non-enforcement—fiscal expenditures on public services, depressed wages for American workers, the administrative costs of managing a shadow population, and the incalculable cost of diminished respect for the rule of law. When these factors are considered, the investment in enforcement is not only justifiable but economically sound.

VII. The Humanitarian Dimension

Critics will argue that mass deportation is inhumane, that it would separate families, disrupt communities, and inflict suffering on millions of people, many of whom have lived in the United States for years and have built lives here. These concerns are not trivial, and any enforcement policy should be implemented with as much procedural fairness and basic human decency as possible.

However, the humanitarian argument against enforcement proves too much. If the passage of time and the establishment of personal ties are sufficient to override the law, then the law has no force at all—anyone who can evade detection long enough effectively earns a right to remain. This is not a legal principle; it is an invitation to continued violation.

Moreover, the humanitarian costs of non-enforcement are routinely ignored. The journey undertaken by illegal border crossers is extraordinarily dangerous—thousands die each year in deserts, rivers, and at the hands of smugglers. The existence of a permissive enforcement environment encourages people to undertake these perilous journeys. Credible, consistent enforcement would deter illegal crossings and, over time, save lives by discouraging people from placing themselves in danger.

The humanitarian concerns associated with deportation, while real, are the predictable consequences of choices made in violation of clearly established law. The responsibility for family separation lies primarily with those who chose to create family ties in a country where they had no legal right to reside, not with the government that eventually enforces the law. A compassionate society can acknowledge the difficulty of these situations while maintaining that the law must ultimately be upheld.

Conclusion

The case for mass deportation rests on principles that are foundational to democratic governance: the rule of law, national sovereignty, fairness, economic justice, and security. These are not partisan principles—they are the preconditions for a functioning republic. For too long, the United States has treated its immigration laws as optional, creating a system that rewards violation, punishes compliance, harms vulnerable workers, compromises security, and erodes public trust in government.

Comprehensive enforcement of immigration law, including the removal of those who are present in the country illegally, is not an act of cruelty—it is an act of governance. It is the reassertion of the principle that in a democratic society, laws enacted by the people's representatives must be carried out, and that the privilege of residing in the United States is conferred through legal processes, not through successful evasion of them.

The challenge is significant, but significance is not impossibility. With political will, strategic investment, and a commitment to both firmness and procedural fairness, the United States can restore the integrity of its immigration system, honor the sacrifices of legal immigrants, protect its most vulnerable workers, secure its borders, and reaffirm the foundational principle that no one—citizen or non-citizen—is above the law. The alternative is the continued erosion of the legal and civic foundations upon which the nation depends.

"The Sovereignty We Owe": A Speech on Immigration Enforcement

Ladies and gentlemen,

There is a principle so fundamental to the existence of any nation that to abandon it is to abandon the very idea of nationhood itself: the rule of law.

Every sovereign country on Earth — every single one — maintains the right to decide who enters its borders, under what conditions, and through what process. This is not radical. This is not extreme. This is the baseline definition of what it means to be a country.

They told us the problem was too big. Too complicated. Too sensitive. They told us enforcement was impractical, that we should simply accept a permanent underclass living outside the legal framework that binds the rest of us.

I'm here today to say: enough.

Let me be direct about what I am advocating.

I am calling for the full, consistent, and humane enforcement of existing immigration law — including the removal of individuals who are present in this country without legal authorization. Not selectively. Not partially. Comprehensively.

And I want to explain why — not with anger, but with conviction.

First: The rule of law must mean something.

A law that is not enforced is not a law. It is a suggestion. And when we tell the world that our immigration laws are merely suggestions, we do not simply invite disorder at the border — we corrode the very foundation of civic trust.

Every legal immigrant — every person who waited years, filled out forms, paid fees, learned English, studied our civics, and followed the process — is dishonored when we shrug our shoulders at those who bypassed that process entirely. We owe those legal immigrants better. We owe our own citizens better. We owe the concept of citizenship better.

If our laws are unjust, we change them — through Congress, through debate, through democracy. What we do not do is simply stop enforcing them and pretend the problem doesn't exist.

Second: National sovereignty is not negotiable.

A nation without borders is not a nation. This is not a slogan — it is a geometric truth. The ability to define and defend territorial boundaries, to determine the terms of membership in a political community, is the most elementary function of governance.

When we permit millions of people to live and work here outside any legal framework, we have effectively surrendered control of our immigration system to the decisions of individuals — however sympathetic their circumstances may be — rather than maintaining it as a collective democratic choice. That is an abdication of sovereignty, and the American people never voted for it.

Third: Compassion without order is chaos.

I anticipate the objection: "But these are families. These are hard-working people. They contribute to their communities."

I do not doubt it. I do not question the humanity, the work ethic, or the dreams of any individual. But compassion cannot be the sole organizing principle of immigration policy any more than it can be the sole organizing principle of any legal system. We do not allow people to shoplift because they are hungry without consequence. We do not suspend tax law because someone's circumstances are sympathetic. Compassion must be exercised within a framework of law — otherwise it becomes an instrument of its own destruction.

The truly compassionate approach is to build a system that is clear, fair, consistently enforced, and generous in its legal channels — so that nobody is incentivized to take a dangerous, illegal journey in the first place, and so that no one lives in the shadows, vulnerable to exploitation, unable to fully participate in civic life.

Mass non-enforcement is not compassion. It is neglect disguised as kindness.

Fourth: The costs are real and they are borne by the most vulnerable Americans.

It is not wealthy Americans in gated communities who feel the pressure of uncontrolled immigration. It is working-class Americans — disproportionately Black and Hispanic Americans — who face wage depression in the industries where they compete for jobs. It is public school systems stretched beyond capacity. It is emergency rooms in border communities. It is local governments struggling to provide services.

When we refuse to enforce immigration law, we are asking the most economically vulnerable citizens to absorb the costs while the most privileged enjoy the benefits. That is not justice. That is a transfer of burden from those who can afford to be idealistic to those who cannot.

Fifth: This is about process, not prejudice.

Let me say this as clearly as I can: This is not about race. This is not about ethnicity. This is not about where someone comes from.

This is about how someone comes. Through the legal front door, or outside the law entirely. That distinction has nothing to do with skin color and everything to do with whether we are a nation of laws or a nation of exceptions.

I welcome — enthusiastically, patriotically — every person of every background who comes to the United States through lawful means. I want more legal immigration. I want faster processing. I want a system that works. But the prerequisite for a functional legal system is the enforcement of that system. You cannot reform what you refuse to enforce.

So what am I calling for?

I am calling for:

  1. The systematic identification and removal of individuals unlawfully present — prioritized by criminal record, but ultimately comprehensive, because the law does not apply only to those we find most unsympathetic.

  2. Massive investment in immigration courts — to ensure that every case is heard, that due process is respected, and that removals are conducted lawfully and humanely.

  3. Robust border security — physical barriers where effective, technology where appropriate, and personnel sufficient to the task — so that enforcement is not an endless cycle.

  4. Severe penalties for employers who knowingly hire unauthorized workers — because if we are serious about enforcement, we must address demand as well as supply.

  5. Reformed and expanded legal immigration channels — so that the message is unmistakable: come legally, and you are welcome; come illegally, and you will be returned.

  6. Humane processing throughout — because enforcement and decency are not opposites. Every person must be treated with dignity, even as the law is applied.

I know this will be called heartless. I know the images will be difficult. I know there will be hard cases — people who have been here for years, who have built lives, who have children.

And I will not pretend those cases are easy. They are not. They are the consequence of decades of failed enforcement — and the longer we wait, the harder those cases become. Every year of inaction creates deeper roots, more complicated lives, more painful separations. The most heartless thing we can do is perpetuate a system that creates these impossible situations by refusing to enforce its own rules.

If we believe certain categories of people deserve a legal path to remain, then pass that law. Put it before Congress. Vote on it. But do not simply refuse to enforce existing law and call that a policy. That is dereliction.

I love this country — not because it is perfect, but because it is ours. It belongs to its citizens. All of them. And the decisions about who joins this national community must be made by those citizens, through their elected representatives, in accordance with the law.

That is not nativism. That is democracy.

Every great nation in history that lost control of its borders lost its ability to govern itself. I do not intend for that to happen here. Not on our watch.

The American people have been patient. They have been told to wait. They have been told it's too hard. They have been called names for simply asking that their own government enforce its own laws.

That patience has run out.

It is time to restore the law. It is time to defend our sovereignty. It is time to build an immigration system that is generous, fair, orderly, and — above all — enforced.

Because a nation that will not enforce its own laws does not deserve to endure. And this nation — this nation — deserves to endure.

Thank you. God bless you, and God bless the United States of America.
